content: The sender is responsible for preparing shipping documents and ensuring their completion. They may provide guidance to the sender on proper packaging methods, assist in determining the most direct routing for the shipment, and confirm the routing. Additionally, they maintain and archive copies of the documentation related to the shipment and transportation process. It is important to note that the shipper must ensure compliance with all relevant regulations when preparing the package and documentation, even if advice has been provided by the carrier. The receiver, also referred to as the consignee, importer, or buyer, must confirm with national authorities that the substance being imported is legally permissible and registered. They are required to obtain the necessary authorizations, such as import permits, from national authorities for receiving the substance. These permits may need to be provided to the sender, as applicable. The receiver is also responsible for arranging the most efficient and timely collection of the shipment upon arrival and must acknowledge receipt to the sender. The consignor is the individual or organization responsible for sending the shipment, commonly referred to as the shipper or sender. The consignee is the individual or organization responsible for receiving the shipment, also known as the receiver or buyer. A consignment refers to a package or group of packages intended for delivery. Both shippers and carriers must adhere to all relevant laws and regulations. Specific responsibilities may be outlined in contractual agreements, such as material transfer agreements (MTAs) or shipping agreements, which can vary significantly depending on the arrangement between the involved parties. Carriers often have limitations on their liability, particularly in cases where damage or loss is not due to their negligence. Insurance is frequently used to manage risks associated with the shipment's contents, damage, or loss. Responsibilities may vary depending on the region, the type of goods being shipped, and the specific arrangements between the parties involved. Before offering a consignment of dangerous goods for transport, all relevant personnel involved in its preparation must receive training to enable them to fulfill their responsibilities. If the organization responsible for preparing the shipment lacks appropriately trained staff, the term relevant persons may include those contracted to act on behalf of the shipper and undertake the shipper's responsibilities in preparing the shipment. However, such individuals must still meet applicable training requirements. Personnel should be trained in accordance with their contractual responsibilities, and the training content should be determined by analyzing their assigned roles and responsibilities as part of their job description. In some cases, this determination is made by the employer, while in others, it is stipulated or governed by national competent authorities. Employees should only perform functions for which they have received the required training or be appropriately supervised and signed off by a competent individual. According to the UN Model Regulations, all individuals involved in the transport of dangerous goods must be trained in the requirements for dangerous goods commensurate with their responsibilities. This training should include general awareness and familiarization with the provisions of dangerous goods transport requirements, such as the classification of dangerous goods, labeling, marking, placarding, segregation, compatibility, documentation, and emergency response procedures. Function-specific training ensures personnel are competent to perform their assigned functions before undertaking them. For example, a shipper at a public health institution may require training on classification, packing, labeling, marking, and documenting dangerous goods, while a carrier may need training on acceptance, handling, loading, stowing, and logistics procedures. Safety training includes the proper use of equipment, emergency response information, prevention of exposure to hazards, and procedures for unintentional releases or spills. Training records must be maintained by the employer and made available upon request by the employee or national competent authority. Training should be periodically supplemented with retraining as deemed necessary by the competent authority, typically every two years. Dangerous goods training programs may be subject to review and approval by relevant national competent authorities. For comprehensive guidance on the safe and compliant shipping of infectious substances, eligible stakeholders can access the World Health Organization's digital Infectious Substances Shipping Training (e-ISST) and refresher courses. These programs provide an overview of international and domestic regulations, packaging requirements, and best practices to ensure the safe transportation of infectious substances. Infectious substances are defined as materials containing pathogens, such as bacteria, viruses, parasites, fungi, or prions, capable of causing disease in humans or animals. Before transportation, it is essential to determine whether the material qualifies as an infectious substance. Examples include cultures, infected live animals, patient specimens, biological products, medical or clinical wastes, and contaminated medical devices or equipment. Each category has specific regulatory requirements for classification, packaging, and documentation. Cultures involve the intentional propagation of biological agents under controlled laboratory conditions, resulting in concentrated collections of pathogens. Infected live animals must be transported in accordance with regulations in the country of origin, transit, and destination. Patient specimens, collected for research or diagnostic purposes, may include blood, tissues, or other biological materials. Biological products, such as vaccines or antitoxins, may be subject to additional licensing or regulatory requirements due to their importance in disease prevention and treatment. Medical or clinical wastes contaminated with infectious agents must be classified and transported according to their risk level, with Category A substances assigned specific UN numbers (e.g., UN 2814, UN 2900, UN 3549). Decontaminated medical or clinical wastes that no longer contain infectious substances are not subject to the UN Model Regulations unless they meet criteria for inclusion in another class of dangerous goods. Contaminated medical devices or equipment may also be classified as infectious substances if they contain agents capable of causing disease. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or microorganisms (GMMOs) that do not meet the definition of toxic or infectious substances must be assigned to UN 3245. COVID-19 vaccines containing GMOs or GMMOs are not subject to Dangerous Goods Regulations.
